newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: BELGIAN MAYSTADT SETS OUT THEMES FOR IMF MEETING.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN MAYSTADT SETS OUT THEMES FOR IMF MEETING.

text.p: Japan's weak economy and Europe's high unemployment will be key themes when the IMF and World Bank meet in Washington this month, Philippe Maystadt, head of the IMF's policy-making interim committee, said on Sunday.
Maystadt, who is Belgium's Finance Minister, said there was no consensus on what Japan should do to spark its economy into life.
"There are some who say it must continue fiscal consolidation, others who say that this is braking the recovery," he told Reuters in an interview after a meeting of European Union finance ministers.
The International Monetary Fund was expected to reiterate a call for greater labour market flexibility in Europe, in order to tackle unemployment running at post-war records in many countries.

And countries outside Europe would be looking for reassurance that the region's plans to launch a single currency in 1999 would not be preceded by financial market turbulence that would spread beyond the region.
Japan's economic weakness and Europe's unemployment are seen by economists as two of the major threats to an otherwise reasonably healthy outlook for economic growth in the industrialised world.

Both are recurring topics among ministers in the Group of Seven (G7) rich industrialised nations, amid questions about how strong a dollar the United States is prepared to tolerate, while its trading partners in Europe and Japan cash in on the benefit to their exports of relatively weaker currencies.
G7 finance ministers will meet in Washington on April 26 ahead of the half-yearly meeting of the IMF and World Bank.
At their last meeting in Berlin in February they indicated they wanted exchange rates to stabilise at current levels.
Maystadt said the Fund would look again at the plight of poor nations marginalised by the rush to "globalisation" -- the increasing interdependency of world markets as trade barriers drop.
He said he hoped there would be a decision on providing debt relief to at least one country under an initiative agreed last year to help poor heavily indebted nations.

The IMF, World Bank and Paris Club of creditor nations agreed last year to work together on a joint debt relief initiative to help countries which have implemented economic reforms, but for whom all the benefits of improved growth are eaten up by heavy debt service charges.
Yet, although officials had hoped to put the plan into action before the end of 1996, it has not happened yet.
Maystadt said work was completed to give Uganda enhanced debt relief and considerable progress had been made on providing it to Bolivia, Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast.
"We ought to be able to decide on Uganda. The dossier is ready for a decision," he said. "We could be well advanced towards a decision on another country."

In Addis Ababa last week, however, diplomats attending a meeting of African finance officials said concern about a rise in Uganda's military spending could delay plans to make it the first beneficiary of the debt initiative.
Maystadt said the IMF will also discuss for the first time the sensitive issue of requiring all members to fully liberalise capital movements.

He said there was a broad majority in favour of this, though key details had to be agreed, notably over whether IMF funds would be used to help some countries over the initial impact of opening up their capital markets.

IMF members would also have to agree how quickly capital movements should be freed up, amid fears that too rapid a liberalisation would expose some countries to big destabilising shifts in money flows.
And they would look at whether liberalisation would apply to all capital movements, including inward direct investment.
Maystadt said he did not expect a decision on liberalising capital movements, which will require a change in the IMF's statutes, in April.
